summary: Discusses how existing IP Operations, Administration, and Maintenance protocols and mechanisms can be used in Deterministic Networking networks with the IP data plane. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This looks at which existing network checking tools can help a promised-delivery network that uses ordinary internet packets.

questions: how do you test a network that must deliver packets on time
can you use ping and traceroute in a detnet network
subtitle: Testing and managing networks that promise to deliver packets on time.

tldr.problem: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) promises guaranteed on-time packet delivery for critical applications like industrial automation and vehicle control. Unlike best-effort networks, DetNet needs precise monitoring and fault detection to ensure promised delivery times are met. Operations staff must verify that the network is behaving correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how existing IP-based Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) tools—such as ICMP, BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection), and STAMP (Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol)—can be applied to DetNet networks. The key is ensuring OAM test packets follow the exact same network path and receive the same priority treatment as the user data flows they are testing.
tldr.outcome: By mapping OAM sessions to DetNet flows and using proper encapsulation (such as DetNet-in-UDP tunnels), operators can detect failures and measure performance in guaranteed-delivery networks without deploying new tools. The protocol offers practical guidance for making existing OAM work in time-sensitive environments.

facts.label: Main requirement
facts.value: OAM packets follow same path and QoS as user data

today: RFC 9634 is an Informational RFC published by the IETF in October 2024. It reflects current practice: existing OAM tools can be adapted for DetNet by careful provisioning and encapsulation. The RFC acknowledges that DetNet OAM is an open engineering problem with no single perfect solution; different encapsulation methods suit different deployment scenarios. No new protocols are required, but operators must understand how to map legacy OAM tools to guaranteed-delivery networks.

sections.title: Why OAM Matters in Deterministic Networks
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking guarantees that packets travel through the network in bounded time with minimal loss, making it suitable for critical applications: industrial automation, vehicle control systems, and real-time audio/video. Unlike the best-effort Internet, where some packets may be delayed or dropped and applications adapt, DetNet applications depend on these guarantees.

Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) tools detect failures, localize problems, and measure performance. In a best-effort network, OAM is nice to have. In DetNet, it is essential: operators must verify that the network is actually meeting its promises. A failure in a DetNet network is not just slow service; it could mean a missed deadline, a safety violation, or a broken system.

The challenge is that DetNet uses special forwarding rules to ensure bounded delay. OAM test packets must follow the same path as user data and receive the same priority, or the test results will be misleading. This document explains how to use existing IP OAM protocols in DetNet networks with the IP data plane.
sections.eli5: A network that promises to deliver packets fast needs tools to check that the promise is kept. If you test with packets that get different treatment than real data, the test lies to you. This document shows how to test the right way.

sections.title: OAM Protocols and Mapping to Flows
sections.content:
Existing IP OAM protocols include ICMP (used for ping and traceroute), BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, for rapid failure detection), and STAMP (Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol, for delay and loss measurement). These protocols work by sending specially crafted test packets that trigger responses, allowing operators to probe the network.

The fundamental challenge is that DetNet routers forward packets based on specific identifiers called flows. A flow might be identified by a tuple of (source IP, destination IP, protocol type, source port, destination port). User data packets in a DetNet flow follow a carefully provisioned path with reserved bandwidth and bounded delay.

For OAM to work, test packets must be mapped to the same flow as the user data. If an OAM packet uses different port numbers or IP addresses, it may take a different path or receive different treatment, making test results invalid. The solution is to carefully choose the IP and UDP headers of OAM packets so they match the DetNet flow being tested, or to encapsulate them in a tunnel that itself matches the flow.
sections.eli5: A network treats packets differently depending on where they come from and where they go. To test a route, your test packet needs to look like the real packets so it gets the same treatment. Otherwise, your test does not tell you anything useful.

sections.title: Encapsulation Techniques
sections.content:
The RFC describes several ways to encapsulate OAM packets so they follow DetNet flows:

Direct IP-level mapping: OAM protocols like BFD use UDP with well-known port numbers (e.g., port 4784 for multihop BFD). A router can identify a BFD test packet as belonging to a DetNet flow by matching the flow's source and destination IPs, protocol type, and UDP port numbers. This requires the least overhead but requires careful coordination of port numbers.

IP-in-UDP tunneling: An entire IP packet (including ICMP or other OAM protocol) can be encapsulated inside a UDP packet. The outer UDP/IP headers are chosen to match the DetNet flow, so the tunnel itself gets the right treatment. The DetNet network sees only the outer headers and forwards accordingly. This adds overhead but provides flexibility: the inner OAM packet can use any protocol.

DetNet-in-UDP tunneling: FROST (Packet Replication, Elimination, and Ordering Functions) encapsulation is used to ensure OAM test packets follow the exact same path within the DetNet service layer as user data. This is the most robust approach for networks using PREOF redundancy.

GRE-in-UDP for Y.1731: The Y.1731 Ethernet OAM protocol can be carried inside Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) inside UDP. This allows using a comprehensive OAM toolkit (continuity checks, loss measurement, delay measurement) while meeting DetNet routing requirements.
sections.eli5: You can send OAM test packets inside a DetNet-compatible tunnel so they get routed the same way as real data. Different tunneling methods work for different situations: some are simple, others are more robust for special features like redundancy.

sections.title: Connecting DetNet with Other Networks
sections.content:
A DetNet network does not stand alone. It might need to deliver packets through Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) domains (for wired local-area connectivity in industrial settings) or MPLS DetNet domains (for WAN interconnection). When DetNet with the IP data plane interworks with these other technologies, OAM must also interwork.

The RFC identifies two interworking models: peering (where DetNet and the other network exchange information directly) and tunneling (where DetNet encapsulates traffic for the other network). In either case, OAM functions must be preserved: the ability to detect faults and measure performance must carry through the entire path.

For IP DetNet interworking with MPLS DetNet or TSN, the same OAM mapping principles apply: test packets must be provisioned so they follow the same path and receive the same treatment as user data across all network domains.
sections.eli5: A DetNet network might connect to other special-delivery networks. When it does, the monitoring has to work end-to-end. A packet might go through DetNet, then TSN, then MPLS. The test packets need to follow the same route all the way.
